clue.text: Opening part of the Bible studied by an actor

indicators.note: only the front portion of the word for the holy book is kept, its tail of three letters dropped

parts.note: the Bible is Holy Scripture

explanation.surface: An actor reads the first verses of Genesis as a rehearsal piece.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor learns the lines of a play's text before performing.

clue.text: Army officer and politician join queue for an hour of prayer

parts.note: CO is a commanding officer
MP is a member of Parliament
a line is a queue

explanation.surface: A soldier and a politician wait in line before evening prayers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'join' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The last of the canonical hours, the night service of the Church.

clue.text: For its runners the going of course must be hard

definitions.text: For its runners the going of course must be hard

parts.words: For its runners the going of course must be hard
parts.note: it sounds like horse racing on firm turf, but the runners are skates on a frozen course

explanation.surface: A racehorse trainer insisting that his runners need firm ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going' is horse-racing jargon for ground conditions; here the vessel's runners need ice.
explanation.definitionFit: A sailing craft on runners that skims over frozen water.

clue.text: Unimportantly, score appears about right — four-one

indicators.note: one word goes round others, so the count is put about the letters

parts.note: to score is to keep a tally
IV is four and I is one in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A trivial result: the score is about right at four-one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appears' is a link; TALLY goes 'about' R and IVI.
explanation.definitionFit: In a petty or insignificant way.

clue.text: Boys lost, misdirected by this crafty fellow

indicators.note: sent the wrong way, so the letters of the two words are set off in a new order

explanation.surface: A cunning man has led some boys astray, and now they are lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misdirected' turns the letters of BOYS LOST into the answer; 'by this' links the anagram to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An old informal word for a sly, artful person.

clue.text: It's said Hamlet's last word betrays the Midas touch

parts.note: Hamlet dies saying 'The rest is silence'
everything King Midas touched turned to gold, so it shows itself golden

explanation.surface: Hamlet's dying word reveals the golden touch of Midas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's said' defines the answer as a saying, a proverb.
explanation.definitionFit: A proverb, a familiar saying recommending discretion.

clue.text: Old sword-bearer, no end wealthy if lacking capital cover at first

indicators.note: at first means this part comes before the rest

parts.note: capital is the head, so bald is lacking hair on top

indicators.note: no end means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: wealthy means rich

explanation.surface: An old swordsman is extremely rich, if only his head is uncovered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no end' looks like 'extremely' wealthy but means cutting the last letter of RICH; 'if' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A baldric is a shoulder belt for carrying a sword.

clue.text: Aid a merger to provide such entertainment

definitions.text: Aid a merger to provide such entertainment

parts.words: Aid a merger to provide such entertainment
parts.note: run the first two words together and you get Verdi's work, an example of the art in question

explanation.surface: Help a company merger to stage a show.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to opera, the stage art of which Verdi's Aida is an example.

clue.text: Such (sic) was the curtiosity (sic) of Kipling's young elephant

definitions.text: Such (sic) was the curtiosity (sic) of Kipling's young elephant

parts.words: Such (sic) was the curtiosity (sic) of Kipling's young elephant
parts.note: the Just So story of the Elephant's Child describes his curiosity with a shortened form of ... and a misspelling

explanation.surface: A quotation from Kipling about an inquisitive baby elephant.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's Elephant's Child was 'full of 'satiable curtiosity'; the (sic) marks flag the odd spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Here a clipped form meaning insatiable, never satisfied.

clue.text: Put in danger accepting article describing Caesar's rule

indicators.note: one word takes in another, so the article sits inside the verb

parts.note: to put in danger is to imperil
A is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Someone endangered by taking on a piece of writing about how Caesar governed.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar's rule was that of an emperor, and this adjective means belonging to an empire.

clue.text: But this memorial did not commemorate the Blackpool lion's victim

definitions.text: But this memorial did not commemorate the Blackpool lion's victim

parts.words: But this memorial did not commemorate the Blackpool lion's victim
parts.note: a London memorial to Queen Victoria's consort shares its name with the boy swallowed by Wallace the lion at Blackpool zoo in a famous comic monologue

explanation.surface: A grand monument that, despite its name, honours not a boy eaten at the zoo.
explanation.walkthrough: In Marriott Edgar's monologue 'The Lion and Albert', a boy at Blackpool (a northern English seaside resort) is swallowed by a lion; the London memorial of the same name honours Prince Albert instead.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is shared by Victoria's husband, whose memorial stands in Kensington, and the monologue's boy.

clue.text: German shepherd was one taking sanctuary in Whitefriars

definitions.meaning: the large dog breed also called a German shepherd

definitions.text: was one taking sanctuary in Whitefriars
definitions.meaning: Alsatia was the old cant name for Whitefriars in London, a sanctuary for debtors and criminals, whose inhabitants took this name

explanation.surface: A German herdsman who once hid from the law in a London district.
explanation.walkthrough: Whitefriars, between Fleet Street and the Thames, kept the right of sanctuary into the 17th century and was nicknamed after the disputed border province Alsace.
explanation.definitionFit: The dog breed and a dweller in that lawless London refuge share one name.

clue.text: Prepare girl for battle in the fleet

parts.note: to arm is to prepare for battle
Ada is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl gets ready to fight among the warships.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for battle' completes the sense of 'Prepare': to arm someone is to make them ready to fight.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish Armada was a war fleet; the word means a fleet of warships.

clue.text: A bad don, in a word, taking unusual cine of Greece

parts.words: A bad don, in a word
parts.note: summed up in a single word, a dreadful tutor is hell to endure

indicators.note: unusual signals that the four letters are put into an odd order

explanation.surface: A disreputable academic, briefly put, watching a strange Greek film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' scrambles the film word into ENIC. 'A bad don, in a word' is an odd phrase: a dreadful academic summed up as one word of judgement; 'taking' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means Greek, from Hellas, the Greek name for Greece.

clue.text: Clever to be at home with a brilliant brain? Nothing in it

parts.note: to be at home is to be in

indicators.note: one piece set within the other

parts.note: a genius is a brilliant mind
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Is it clever to sit at home with a great mind, when there's nothing to it?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing in it' puts O inside GENIUS; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Inventive and resourceful, showing clever thinking.

clue.text: Best or worst round for Bobby?

definitions.meaning: to best someone is to defeat them
to worst someone is also to defeat them
a bobby is a British policeman, and his regular round is his patrol

explanation.surface: Asking which patrol route is the finest or the poorest for a policeman.
explanation.walkthrough: Three definitions: 'Best' and 'worst' look like opposites but both are verbs meaning defeat. BOBBY is British slang for a police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means overcome and also a constable's patrol area.

clue.text: Sign put up about drinking-place one finds uncouth

indicators.note: the reversed sign goes round the rest
in a down clue put up means written from bottom to top

parts.note: the Crab is Cancer, a sign of the zodiac
a bar is a drinking place
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A sign hung over a pub that someone finds coarse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' turns CRAB to BARC, which goes 'about' BAR and I; 'finds' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Savage and uncivilised, crude in manners.

clue.text: A private army to have ringleader who stirs up trouble

parts.note: a GI is an American private soldier
TA is the Territorial Army
taken as written
the leader of the word ring is its first letter

explanation.surface: A private soldier forms an army with a ringleader who causes unrest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'have' is a link. TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: An agitator is someone who stirs up trouble, a rabble-rouser.

clue.text: Facial blemishes 'eard of in East London

indicators.note: dropping the h in the Cockney way, a place name spoken there becomes a skin complaint

parts.note: Hackney is a borough in East London

explanation.surface: Spots on the face are reported among Cockneys.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys famously drop the H, so 'Hackney', a district of East London, comes out as 'ackney'; the clue's own ''eard' shows the dropped H.
explanation.definitionFit: A skin condition marked by spots and pimples, typically on the face.

clue.text: A mausoleum mob: destroyed with high explosive

parts.note: a mausoleum is a grand tomb

indicators.note: destroyed means the letters of mob are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A mob tears down a mausoleum with powerful explosives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'destroyed' rearranges MOB to OMB; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A nuclear weapon, the most powerful kind of explosive device.

clue.text: South African province supporting maybe one of newborn children

indicators.note: in a down clue, the province sits below and holds up the other piece
maybe suggests the letters of one could be arranged otherwise

parts.note: Natal was a province of South Africa

explanation.surface: A South African province backing one of its newborn babies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' rearranges ONE to NEO, with NATAL 'supporting' it below.
explanation.definitionFit: Neonatal means relating to babies in their first weeks.

clue.text: By which one sees there's agreement among the crew

definitions.text: By which one sees there's agreement among the crew

parts.words: By which one sees there's agreement among the crew
parts.note: it is the faculty of vision, and spoken it is a rowing boat's crew all voting yes

explanation.surface: How a captain spots that the team are all of one mind.
explanation.walkthrough: AYES are yes votes and an EIGHT is a rowing crew; said together they make the word for vision.
explanation.definitionFit: The faculty of seeing with one's eyes.

clue.text: As unending as Pope's hope

definitions.meaning: Alexander Pope wrote 'Hope springs ... in the human breast'

explanation.surface: Asking whether something is as endless as the hope in a famous line.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet Alexander Pope, not a pontiff: in An Essay on Man he says hope springs this way.
explanation.definitionFit: Eternal means lasting for ever; Pope's line calls hope so.

clue.text: Improved as a poker-player for instance

definitions.meaning: made superior, raised to a higher standard
a poker player is one who wagers money

explanation.surface: Someone who has become more skilled at poker.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means more good, and also a gambler who places stakes.

clue.text: Novel manner to get decoration

indicators.note: novel means new, so these letters take a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A fresh style of writing earns an award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book, but signals rearranging MANNER and TO; 'get' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An ornament is an embellishment or adornment.

clue.text: Backing for a pupil

parts.note: not support for a schoolchild but the light-sensitive layer behind the eye's opening

explanation.surface: Support for a schoolchild.
explanation.definitionFit: The light-sensitive membrane lining the back of the eye, behind the opening of the iris.

clue.text: Boss, returning, receives terribly poor refugees from society

indicators.note: one piece takes another inside it
coming back, so the word for boss is read from right to left

parts.note: a stud is a boss, a raised knob

indicators.note: terribly means the letters of the word poor are badly jumbled

explanation.surface: A returning manager takes in desperately needy people who have left society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' reverses STUD to DUTS; 'terribly' makes ROPO from POOR, which DUTS 'receives'. Boss here is a decorative knob, not an employer.
explanation.definitionFit: People who have opted out of conventional society, as in the 1960s.

clue.text: Laurence turning blue

indicators.note: turning round its letters gives a different word

explanation.surface: A man called Laurence goes blue in the face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' rearranges LAURENCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Cerulean is a deep sky blue.

clue.text: Cunning to omit it from the translation screened

indicators.note: omit means a short word is taken out of the longer one

parts.note: a subtitle is a translation shown on screen
taken as written

explanation.surface: A clever move is leaving something out of a film's translation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' links the removal to the word removed from.
explanation.definitionFit: Subtle here means crafty and sly, as in a subtle plan.
